The pursuit now degenerated into a sauve pui peut rout, from which our sources salvage one or two famous individual episodes.

We glimpse a pair of erstwhile rivals turned allies, Polycritus of Aegina and Themistocles, the latter aboard his emblazoned Admiral's galley, racing neck-and-neck down-channel, while Polycritus -- having just scuppered an enemy vessel -- yells across, half-cocky, half-defensive: 'Who said Aegina was pro-Persian?"

We see Artemisia of Halicarnassus, hotly pursued by a trireme from the Attica squadron, cram on all speed and ruthlessly run down one of her own side, a vessel commanded by some Carian princeling from nearby Calynda.

'I cannot say', Herodotus observes demurely, 'if she did this deliberately because of some quarrel she had with this man... or if it was just chance that that particular vessel was in the way.'

At all events, she did doubly well out of the error. Her assailant -- that same Ameinias of Pallene who had attacked the Phoenician Admiral's flagship at the onset of the engagement -- observing what had happened, came to the conclusion that his quarry was either a Greek or a deserter fighting on the Greek side, and turned off in search for some other victim. (Xerxes, in the mistaken belief that she had actually sunk an enemy ship, now made his celebrated mot: 'My men have turned into women, my women into men.')

Ameinias was out of his mind with rage and frustration when he learnt the truth, since the Athenians (who disliked the idea of a woman taking up arms against them) had put a 10,000-drachma price on Artemisia's head, and given their captains special instructions to capture her at all costs.

From a general investment angle: keep in mind that just because a business is doing well doesn't mean it's a good idea to buy their stock. You need to evaluate how much they can grow, and at what price they are already trading. Do you have a good insight into the industry the company is operating in, which could give you an advantage over other investors? If you don't, then the default assumption should be that the market valuation of the stock is roughly correct. You can buy their stock and if you are holding on to it for the long run, you'll likely make good money. However you are taking on more risk than if you are buying an index fund, and chances are that your returns will not exceed those of an index fund.
